stories.headline: Trump abruptly postpones AI executive order after last-minute tech-industry lobbying

key_facts.fact: Trump called off a Thursday (May 21) Oval Office ceremony to sign a new AI and cybersecurity executive order, saying he disliked the draft text: 'Because I didn't like certain aspects of it, I postponed it ... we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead.'
key_facts.excerpt: "Because I didn't like certain aspects of it, I postponed it," Mr. Trump said ... "I think it gets in the way of, you know, we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead."

key_facts.fact: The draft order would have tasked the Office of the National Cyber Director and other agencies with building a process to evaluate AI models for security before release; a key sticking point was a proposed voluntary framework asking AI developers to share 'covered frontier models' with the government between 14 and 90 days ahead of launch.
key_facts.excerpt: The anticipated executive order would have tasked the Office of the National Cyber Director and other agencies with developing a process to evaluate AI models for security before their release ... a proposed requirement for AI companies to share advanced models with the government between 14 and 90 days ahead of launch.

key_facts.fact: The push for pre-release vetting followed concern over the cyber capabilities of Anthropic's Mythos model and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber, both of which can quickly find and exploit software vulnerabilities.
key_facts.excerpt: This is partly in response to concerns from the release of Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber - both of which can quickly find and exploit security vulnerabilities.

key_facts.fact: Four sources told Politico the delay was due in part to leading tech executives being unable to attend on short notice; some CEOs had been invited and were reportedly already midair en route to Washington when the White House reversed course.
key_facts.excerpt: top tech executives had been invited to the signing ceremony - some were even midair, en route to Washington. Then, hours before the signing, the White House abruptly reversed course, postponing the executive order.

key_facts.fact: The Washington Post reported that last-minute calls from Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and David Sacks helped persuade Trump not to sign, with Sacks telling the president that federal pre-release reviews would slow innovation and hurt the US in its AI race with China.
key_facts.excerpt: Industry leaders warned in last-minute calls to the president that the proposed safety vetting system could inhibit development of the pivotal technology.

stories.headline: OpenAI out-earned Anthropic by ~$1B in Q1 but lost $1.22 per dollar as ChatGPT growth stalled

key_facts.fact: OpenAI generated about $5.7 billion in first-quarter revenue, roughly $1 billion more than Anthropic's $4.8 billion, according to The Information.
key_facts.excerpt: OpenAI generated $5.7 billion in revenue during the first quarter, beating Anthropic's $4.8 billion by about $1 billion as the two leading AI labs continue to race toward possible public listings, according to The Information.

key_facts.fact: OpenAI's adjusted operating income margin was -122% in Q1, meaning it lost $1.22 for every $1 of revenue, even after excluding stock-based compensation.
key_facts.excerpt: its adjusted operating income margin stood at minus 122% in the first quarter, which means they lost $1.22 for every dollar of revenue. This despite excluding some important items like the stock-based compensation.

key_facts.fact: ChatGPT user growth stalled at roughly 905 million average weekly active users, while paying subscribers rose to 55 million from 47 million at the end of the prior year.
key_facts.excerpt: OpenAI's user growth stalled at roughly 905 million average weekly active users, while paying subscribers rose to 55 million from 47 million at year end, according to the report.

key_facts.fact: Revenue growth was helped by the Codex coding agent, business sales and early advertising tests on ChatGPT, keeping the company on track for its 2026 goal of $30 billion in revenue; the disclosure landed roughly 12 hours after Anthropic projected $10.9 billion in Q2 revenue and its first operating profit.
key_facts.excerpt: the OpenAI reportedly grew revenues from its coding agent Codex and via business sales and tests of advertising on ChatGPT ... these numbers suggest that the company remained on target to meet its goal of $30 billion revenues in 2026. By the way, Anthropic said its Q2 revenues would be in the region of $10.9 billion.

stories.headline: Cursor hits $3B annualized revenue rate with 3,000+ enterprise customers paying $100K+ each

key_facts.excerpt: Cursor reached $3B in annualized revenue in late April and now has 3,000+ customers paying at least $100K each for its software on an annualized basis.

key_facts.fact: Cursor now has more than 3,000 customers each paying at least $100,000 per year for its software on an annualized basis.
key_facts.excerpt: now has 3,000+ customers paying at least $100K each for its software on an annualized basis

key_facts.fact: The milestone comes as SpaceX holds an option, announced April 21 on X, to acquire Cursor's parent Anysphere for $60 billion later in 2026 (or pay $10 billion for joint work if it declines); Cursor had crossed a $2 billion annualized revenue rate by February 2026 and is used by more than half of the Fortune 500.

stories.headline: Brett Adcock's secretive AI lab Hark raises $700M+ Series A at $6B valuation

key_facts.fact: Hark, an AI lab building models and hardware for a personal AI assistant, said on May 21 it raised over $700 million in an oversubscribed Series A at a $6 billion post-money valuation, led by Parkway Venture Capital.
key_facts.excerpt: Hark ... said on Thursday that it had raised that much in a Series A round that values it at $6 billion post-money. The mega-round was led by Parkway Venture Capital.

key_facts.fact: Investors included Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Intel Capital, Qualcomm Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, ARK Invest, Brookfield, Greycroft, Align Ventures, Prime Movers Lab and Tamarack Global.
key_facts.excerpt: The round was led by Parkway Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Align Ventures, AMD Ventures, ARK Invest, Brookfield, Greycroft, Intel Capital, Prime Movers Lab, Qualcomm Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, and Tamarack Global.

key_facts.fact: Hark was founded in late 2025 by Brett Adcock - also CEO of robotics firm Figure AI and founder of electric-aircraft maker Archer - with $100 million of his own money, to build an agentic AI system that serves as a universal interface to the digital world.
key_facts.excerpt: Founder and CEO, Brett Adcock, also the entrepreneur behind robotics company Figure.AI and electric aircraft builder Archer, launched Hark in late 2025 with $100 million of his own money to develop an agentic AI system that serves as a universal interface with the digital world.

key_facts.fact: The San Jose company currently has 70 employees and runs a data center with Nvidia B200 GPUs; its first software-based AI models are scheduled to debut in summer 2026, with bespoke hardware devices to follow.
key_facts.excerpt: Hark's first software-based AI models are scheduled to debut in Summer 2026, with bespoke hardware devices to follow.

stories.headline: AI designs first custom miniproteins to switch GPCR drug targets on and off, in Nature

key_facts.fact: A study published May 21 in Nature by the UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design and Skape Bio shows for the first time that AI can design proteins to activate or block G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), one of the most important and hardest-to-target classes of drug targets.
key_facts.excerpt: The UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design and Skape Bio led a new study showing for the first time that AI can be used to create computationally designed proteins to activate or block GPCRs. Their findings are published in Nature.

key_facts.fact: The team generated functional lead molecules - both agonists and antagonists - against 11 GPCR targets, including receptors implicated in cancer, diabetes, obesity, migraine, itch and pain.
key_facts.excerpt: the team generated agonists for receptors involved in itch and pain, and antagonists for receptors implicated in cancer, metabolic disease such as diabetes and obesity, and migraine.

key_facts.fact: Cryo-EM structures of five designed miniproteins closely matched their computational models, and in one mouse study a designed miniprotein performed comparably to a clinically used drug while showing fewer side effects.
key_facts.excerpt: Cryo-EM structures of five designed miniproteins closely matched their computational models, underscoring the accuracy of the design pipeline. In one mouse study, a [designed miniprotein performed] comparable to a [clinical drug].

key_facts.fact: The researchers also built a new high-throughput 'receptor diversion' screening system that can test up to 100,000 designs against full-length GPCRs in living human cells, keeping receptors in their native membrane environment.
key_facts.excerpt: a new high-throughput screening system that tests designed proteins against full-length GPCRs in living human cells. The system can evaluate up to 100,000 designs while keeping the receptors in their natural membrane environment.

stories.headline: Newsom signs first-of-its-kind order to shield California workers from AI job displacement

key_facts.fact: On May 21, Governor Gavin Newsom signed what his office called a 'first-of-its-kind' executive order directing California state agencies to work with labor groups, academics and the AI industry to prepare for AI-driven workforce disruption.
key_facts.excerpt: Governor Gavin Newsom today ordered state officials to begin exploring a massive overhaul of its labor policies ... The executive order is the first of its kind signed by any U.S. official, and orders state agencies to collaborate with labor groups, academics and the AI industry.

key_facts.fact: The order directs agencies to study possible subsidies for companies that retain workers instead of replacing them with AI, along with expanded retraining (especially for customer-service, sales and software-development roles), revised severance standards and expanded unemployment insurance.
key_facts.excerpt: look at possible subsidies for companies that retain workers instead of replacing them with autonomous machines ... expanded retraining programs, especially for workers in areas such as customer service, market and sales and software development roles.

key_facts.fact: The more than dozen directives also include a study into universal basic income and 'universal basic capital' - giving every Californian a stake in assets such as corporate stocks, bonds and wealth funds.
key_facts.excerpt: a concept the governor called 'universal basic capital,' giving all residents a stake in assets such as corporate stocks, bonds or wealth funds.

key_facts.fact: The order follows a March 2026 Newsom order requiring vetting of AI companies that do business with the state, and may conflict with the Trump administration's hands-off approach and its push to preempt state AI rules.
key_facts.excerpt: In March, Newsom signed an order aimed at public safety regulations for AI companies that do business with the state. It may come into conflict with the federal government's current stance on AI, however. The Trump administration has broadly advocated for a hands-off approach.
